7ff59ed2e638: The judgment was pronounced three days later, on Monday 14 April at four in the afternoon, in the extraordinary court at the district office: [S122, S123]
2db7f3d9a279: <t1>It is therefore adjudged:</t1> Thomas Nielsen Silkjær shall be punished with hard labour in the house of correction for <t2>Eighteen Months</t2>. Christine Oline Enevoldsen shall be punished with simple imprisonment for one month, but the execution of the sentence is suspended and the sentence lapses after the expiry of 5 years from the pronouncement of this judgment, provided the conditions laid down in § 20 of the provisional Penal Code of 1 April 1911 are fulfilled.
a3076d9eeeae: The judgment repeats the admission of seduction almost word for word — <t1>“must be said to have seduced her into the immoral relationship that took place between them”</t1> — and establishes that neither of them had been charged before. The legal basis is § 162 of the Penal Code for both of them; in her case <t2>“taken together with §§ 21 and 37”</t2>. The two sections are the law’s provisions for the young, from 1866, and the arithmetic comes out exactly: § 162 set the minimum penalty for a stepchild at two months’ simple imprisonment in mitigating circumstances, and § 37 allowed the penalty for anyone between fifteen and eighteen at the time of the offence to be reduced <t3>“by up to half”</t3> — one month, exactly what she was given. § 21 at the same time forbade putting anyone under eighteen in prison on bread and water. And the suspension on top is the suspended sentence — introduced in Denmark in 1905 as something new and continued in the provisional Penal Code of 1 April 1911, whose § 20 the judgment cites. The court expressly grounded it in her young age. In other words, the judge went to the very bottom of what the law allowed at all. [S122, S128]
0224980031cf: The court’s own draft of the judgment — the draft preserved among the documents for the justice registers — shows that precisely those lines came into being along the way. The reference <t1>“in the accused’s case taken together with §§ 21 and 37”</t1> has been added in the margin with an insertion mark. And in the operative part the clerk began on a single joint sentence — <t2>“Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and Christine Oline Enevoldsen shall be punished …”</t2> — before her name was struck out and she was given a sentence of her own, the one with the suspension. The mild outcome was not there in the first stroke of the pen; it was written into being, correction by correction. [S166]

df9b5d8723e3: The period · why was she sentenced too?
3e4367b7d5b5: The Penal Code of 1866 punished <t1>both</t1> parties in what it called incest — even when one was a child in the other’s care. The logic was the period’s: if the girl had not resisted, she was complicit. Only the Penal Code of 1930, in force from 1933, took the younger party out of criminal liability; until then she could be sentenced if she was over the age of criminal responsibility — and mitigation had to be found in the law’s provisions for the young and, from 1905 and with the provisional Penal Code of 1911, in the suspended sentence. Those were exactly the tools this judgment used. [S126, S128]
2ab8b8f9e478: The criminal statistics put figures on it. The decades around 1900 were the provision’s peak: the Statistical Yearbook records between 12 and 18 persons convicted of incest a year nationally in the period 1903—07. The figures count persons, not cases; when both the man and the girl were sentenced, both appear in the statistics — as here. Around the turn of the century about a third of those convicted in cases involving parents and stepparents were women — the great majority of them daughters and stepdaughters, not mothers. [S126, S127]
984451238453: The sentence was mild measured against the courts’ practice of the time. A legal-historical study of incest cases has shown that convicted daughters typically received between eight months and a year in the <t1>house of correction</t1> — up to two years — and that it was usually the girls whose “morality” the court found something to criticise who were sentenced most harshly. She received one month’s simple imprisonment, suspended, with the law’s provisions for the young and § 20 of the provisional Penal Code of 1 April 1911 behind her. And she was among the very few of the very young it struck at all: from 1906, when the age of criminal responsibility was raised to 14, until 1932, only about fifteen persons between 14 and 18 were punished for incest in the whole country. She was one of them. [S126]
e3fa29828144: That the judgment was mild by the standards of its time does not make it reasonable by ours. The law treated her as complicit; the registers themselves — the judge’s word <t1>“attack”</t1>, the man’s admission of seduction, the court’s reference to her age — show that the court could see perfectly well what it was. It sentenced her all the same, because it was in the law — a law that, by her own account, she did not even know existed. [S126, S128, S165]
325182b8ec8f: At Vridsløselille the case became twelve lines. The register of inmates, entry <t1>Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, Husby</t1> — the same man as in the trade’s handbook, the same year of birth, the same occupation. Two hands, two purposes: one was to sell a skipper to his colleagues, the other to describe a prisoner for an institution.
